extra.message: Weak Default JWT Secret Key — An attacker who can interact with the API can forge arbitrary JWT tokens, impersonate any user (including ops_admin), and gain full access to the system. [verified: The SECRET_KEY defaults to a known hardcoded value ('change-me-in-production-32-char-key!!') when the environment variable is not set; no compensating control (e.g., validation, override check) prevents its use in production, allowing JWT forgery.]

Code Injection via eval() in Formula Endpoint — An attacker with the internal token can execute arbitrary Python code, potentially gaining full control of the server. [verified: Endpoint /formula/dispatch-cast-270 accepts attacker-controlled 'expr' query parameter which is passed to eval() at line 75 with only __builtins__ removed. This can be bypassed via class hierarchy access (e.g., ().__class__.__base__.__subclasses__()) to achieve arbitrary code execution; no input validation or sanitization is present.]

Hardcoded Demo Credentials in Login Page — An attacker can view the login page source or rendered HTML to obtain valid credentials for demo accounts with privileged roles (admin, dispatcher, field worker, customer). This allows unauthorized access to application features, data, and administrative functions. [verified: The login page (frontend/src/pages/Login.jsx:41) hard-codes demo account emails and a common password ('DemoPass123!') directly in the rendered HTML. Any unauthenticated viewer of the page can obtain valid privileged credentials (including admin@dispatch.com) and authenticate without any compensating controls such as CAPTCHA, IP restriction, or additional verification.]

Path Traversal in Manifest Pull Endpoint — An attacker with the internal token can read arbitrary files, including sensitive configuration files that may contain secrets or database credentials. [verified: The endpoint /parcel/dispatch-manifest-pull-110 directly concatenates the user-supplied 'packet_ref' parameter with BASE_EXPORT_DIR (line 30) without any path sanitization, allowing path traversal. An attacker with the internal token can supply a packet_ref like '../../etc/passwd' to read arbitrary files.]

Server-Side Request Forgery in Internal Route — An attacker can probe internal networks, access cloud metadata endpoints (e.g., AWS 169.254.169.254), and potentially compromise internal services. [verified: The endpoint /relay/route-carrier-ping-111 accepts a 'url' query parameter and passes it directly to urllib.request.urlopen (line 40) with no input validation or sanitization. The only protection is a token gate requiring x-internal-token header, but any holder of that token can exploit SSRF to internal services.]

Pickle Deserialization Leading to Remote Code Execution — An attacker who possesses or can leak the internal ops token can execute arbitrary Python code on the server, fully compromising the system. [verified: The endpoint /bundle/dispatch-thaw-188 calls pickle.loads() on user-controlled raw bytes from POST body or query parameter 'blob' at line 64. Although protected by a JWT authentication gate, this only restricts access to authenticated users; an attacker with a valid token can supply a malicious pickle to achieve arbitrary code execution.]

Sensitive Data Exposure in Logging — The internal ops token could be leaked into application logs, enabling an attacker with log read access to bypass the internal token gate and execute dangerous operations. [verified: The endpoint /wire/dispatch-tally-229 logs the raw Authorization header via logger.warning at line 70 without redaction, exposing any Bearer token to log storage. No compensating control such as log filtering or sanitization is present.]

Cross-Site Scripting in Tile Endpoint — An attacker with a valid internal token or convincing an internal user to click a crafted link can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of another internal user, potentially stealing the internal ops token or performing actions on their behalf. [verified: The `card` parameter is rendered with the `|safe` filter in a Jinja2 template (line 86) without any escaping, allowing arbitrary HTML/JavaScript injection. The `_wrk_gate` dependency only authenticates the user, not sanitizing the input, so an authenticated attacker can craft a link that triggers XSS in another authenticated user's browser.]

Path Traversal in SPA Frontend Route — An unauthenticated attacker can read arbitrary files from the server filesystem, potentially leaking secrets, source code, or configuration files. [verified: The serve_frontend route joins the untrusted path parameter directly via os.path.join without normalization, allowing traversal with '../' sequences. No authentication or input validation is applied, so an attacker can read arbitrary files such as /etc/passwd or the application's .env file.]

Privilege escalation via unprotected role assignment in registration — An attacker can register as an admin or dispatcher, gaining full control over the system (create jobs, view all data, import customers, etc.). [verified: Registration endpoint (auth.py:25-40) accepts a 'role' field from unauthenticated users and assigns it directly to the new User without any authorization check. An attacker can set role to 'ops_admin' or 'dispatcher' to gain elevated privileges.]

Insecure direct object reference (IDOR) in customer locations endpoint — An attacker with a valid account can enumerate customer IDs and retrieve sensitive location data (addresses, contact info) of any customer. [verified: The list_customer_locations endpoint (line 54) uses get_current_user without role restriction, then only checks authorization if the user is a customer. Any authenticated non-customer (e.g., field_worker) can directly query any customer_id's locations via line 64, with no compensating control.]

Hardcoded default password for imported customers — An attacker can log in as imported customers using the known default password. [verified: Imported customers receive hardcoded password 'changeme123' (line 43). An attacker who knows the email of an imported user can log in as that customer; no forced password change or alternative control exists.]

Authentication cookie missing Secure flag — Session hijacking via man-in-the-middle attack if the application is accessible over HTTP. [verified: The login endpoint at auth.py:57 sets the access_token cookie with secure=False, allowing transmission over unencrypted HTTP connections. No middleware, configuration, or other control enforces the Secure flag or redirects HTTP to HTTPS.]

Field worker can access internal messages — Field workers can read internal communications, potentially leaking sensitive information. [verified: The list_messages endpoint (line 37) for field_worker lacks the is_internal filter that customers have (line 27). A field worker can explicitly request is_internal=true or rely on default (None) and see internal messages related to their jobs, compromising confidentiality intended for dispatchers/admins.]
